title: Satyricon
author: Petronius Arbiter

passages.original: Non est passus Agamemnon me diutius declamare in porticu, quam ipse in schola sudaverat, sed Adulescens inquit quoniam sermonem habes non publici saporis et, quod rarissimum est, amas bonam mentem, non fraudabo te arte secreta. Nihil nimirum in his exercitationibus doctores peccant, qui necesse habent cum insanientibus furere. Nam nisi dixerint quae adulescentuli probent, ut ait Cicero, 'soli in scholis relinquentur.' Sicut ficti adulatores cum cenas divitum captant, nihil prius meditantur quam id quod putant gratissi mum auditoribus fore: nec enim aliter impetrabunt quod petunt, nisi quasdam insidias auribus fecerint: sic eloquentiae magister, nisi tanquam piscator eam imposuerit hamis escam, quam scierit appetituros esse pisciculos, sine spe praedae morabitur in scopulo.
passages.english: Agamemnon did not allow me to go on declaiming in the portico longer than he himself had sweated in the school, but said: "Young man, since your talk is not of the common taste and, what is very rare, you love good sense, I will not cheat you of the secret art. Of course the teachers are not at all at fault in these exercises, since they must rave along with the madmen. For unless they say what the young boys approve of, as Cicero says, 'they will be left alone in their schools.' Just as false flatterers, when they angle for the dinners of the rich, think of nothing before what they suppose will be most pleasing to their hearers (for they will not otherwise obtain what they seek unless they lay certain traps for the ears), so a master of eloquence, unless, like a fisherman, he puts on his hooks the bait he knows the little fish will go for, will wait on his rock with no hope of a catch."

passages.original: Haec aliaque cum effusissimis prosequeremur laudationibus, Rogo inquit Agamemnon mihi carissime, numquid duodecim aerumnas Herculis tenes, aut de Vlixe fabulam, quemadmodum illi Cyclops pollicem forcipe extorsit? Solebam haec ego puer apud Homerum legere. Nam Sibyllam quidem Cumis ego ipse oculis meis vidi in ampulla pendere, et cum illi pueri dicerent: Si/bulla, ti/ qe/leis; respondebat illa: a)poqanei=n qe/lw.
passages.english: While we were following these and other remarks with the most lavish praises, Agamemnon said, "Tell me, my dearest friend, do you know the twelve labours of Hercules, or the story about Ulysses, how the Cyclops twisted out his thumb with pincers? I used to read these things in Homer as a boy. For I myself saw with my own eyes the Sibyl at Cumae hanging in a jar, and when the boys said to her, 'Sibyl, what do you want?' she answered, 'I want to die.'"
passages.notes: The Greek is given in Beta Code transliteration: Σίβυλλα, τί θέλεις; ἀποθανεῖν θέλω. The speaker here is evidently Trimalchio addressing Agamemnon, not Agamemnon himself, despite the text as transmitted; the garbled mythology is part of Trimalchio's characterisation.

passages.original: ab hoc epigrammate coepit poetarum esse mentio diuque summa carminis penes Mopsum Thracem memorata est done Trimalchio Rogo inquit "magister, quid putas inter Ciceronem et Publilium interesse? Ego alterum puto disertiorem fuisse, alterum honestiorem. Quid enim his melius dici potest?
passages.english: From this epigram began talk of poets, and for a long time the highest honours in verse were assigned to Mopsus the Thracian, until Trimalchio said, "Tell me, master, what do you think is the difference between Cicero and Publilius? I think the one was more eloquent, the other more decent. For what could be said better than these [lines]?"
passages.notes: "done" read as "donec". Mopsus the Thracian is not securely identified. Publilius is presumably Publilius Syrus, the mime-writer.

passages.original: Videbatur mihi secundum quietem Priapus dicere: 'Encolpion quod quaeris, scito a me in navem tuam esse perductum. ' Exhorruit Tryphaena et Putes inquit una nos dormiisse; nam et mihi simulacrum Neptuni, quod Baiis in tetrastylo notaveram, videbatur dicere: in nave Lichae Gitona invenies.'Hinc scies inquit Eumolpus Epicurum esse hominem divinum, qui eiusmodi ludibria facetissima ratione condemnat
passages.english: "In my sleep Priapus seemed to say to me: 'As for Encolpius, whom you are seeking, know that he has been brought by me onto your ship.'" Tryphaena shuddered and said, "You would think we had slept together; for to me too the statue of Neptune, which I had noticed in the four-columned shrine at Baiae, seemed to say: 'You will find Giton on Lichas' ship.'" "From this you will know," said Eumolpus, "that Epicurus was a godlike man, who condemns mockeries of this kind with a most witty argument."
passages.notes: The opening speaker is evidently Lichas. Eumolpus' remark appears to break off.

passages.original: Podagrici pedibus suis male dicunt, chiragrici manibus, lippi oculis, et qui offenderunt saepe digitos, quicquid doloris habent, in pedes deferunt: Quid me constricta spectatis fronte Catones damnatisque novae simplicitatis opus?Sermonis puri non tristis gratia ridet,quodque facit populus, candida lingua refert.Nam quis concubitus, Veneris quis gaudia nescit?Quis vetat in tepido membra calere toro?Ipse pater veri doctos Epicurus amare iussit, et hoc vitam dixit habere te/los
passages.english:
People with gout curse their feet, those with arthritis their hands, the bleary-eyed their eyes, and those who have often stubbed their toes blame their feet for whatever pain they have.
Why do you look at me with knitted brows, you Catos,
and condemn a work of fresh simplicity?
The cheerful grace of pure, not gloomy, speech smiles out,
and my candid tongue reports what people do.
For who does not know of lovemaking, who of the joys of Venus?
Who forbids limbs to grow warm in a warm bed?
Epicurus himself, the father of truth, bade the wise to love,
and said that this was life's goal.
passages.notes: Final Greek word τέλος ("goal, end") given in Beta Code.
